title: Everything praise (Psalm 148)
hook: sun, moon, sea monsters, snow, kings and children, praise
carry: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life curiously wrought in secret. Your line was fearfully and wonderfully made. Where did your hand rest, and what did you feel there? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A choir director stands up before the concert and takes the roll. Sopranos? Here. Altos? Here. Tenors, basses? Here. Now keep the roll call going. Angels? Sun and moon? Stars? Here. Sea monsters? Here. Fire, hail, snow, fog, the stormy wind? Here. Mountains, fruit trees, cedars, wild animals, cattle, creeping things, birds? Kings, judges, young men and young women, old people and children? All here. That roll call is Psalm one hundred forty-eight. It doesn't ask who believes, who is important, or who can carry a tune. It calls everything into the choir.
screen: `SOPRANOS? ALTOS?` → `SEA MONSTERS? HAIL?` → `EVERYTHING INTO THE CHOIR.`

segments.voice: The psalm has two halves, like a camera tilting from the sky down to the ground. First, from the heavens: angels, hosts, and then, in the King James Bible, "Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light." Then, from verse seven, the earth: "Praise the LORD from the earth, ye dragons, and all deeps." Dragons. The Hebrew is tanninim, great sea creatures, the same word Genesis uses when God creates the great sea monsters on the fifth day. Creatures that frightened the ancient imagination are in the choir. Then the weather. "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word." A storm, in this psalm, isn't chaos. It's doing what it was told. Then mountains and fruit trees, beasts and creeping things, and finally people, every rank mixed together: "Both young men, and maidens; old men, and children." Kings stand in the same row as kids. Why should a rock or a snowflake praise? One old answer: not with words, but by being what it is. A cedar praises by growing like a cedar. The psalm's list has echoes. In the Greek Bible, the book of Daniel includes a long song of three young men in a furnace, calling on everything from frost to whales to bless the Lord; Catholics and Orthodox read it as scripture, and Anglicans sing it as the Benedicite. And Francis of Assisi wrote his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon. Today's hymn All Creatures of Our God and King comes from it.
screen: `FROM THE HEAVENS: SUN AND MOON` · `FROM THE EARTH: SEA MONSTERS` · `STORMY WIND FULFILLING HIS WORD` · `KINGS IN THE SAME ROW AS CHILDREN` · then, large: `PRAISE YE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name ten things in creation. Slowly, one at a time, out loud or in your head. Look around first, then let your mind travel. The light in the window. A cloud. A crow. A tree you pass every day. Rain. Your grandmother's hands. A child somewhere laughing. Something huge, something tiny. Give each one a breath before you move on. When you reach ten, sit with the whole crowd of them. If you pray, you can let each name be a small praise. If you don't, simply let the list be wonder. The bell holds the time.
Everything praise. Psalm one hundred forty-eight's roll call: angels, stars, sea monsters, hail, cedars, kings and children, all called into one choir.
Your line: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar. Today, pick one ordinary thing, the weather, a tree, a puddle, and imagine it singing simply by being itself. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 439 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LET EVERYTHING THAT HAS BREATH.`

howItsDone: Psalm 148 is a traditional morning praise psalm in many churches, and it is echoed in the Benedicite canticle and in hymns such as "All Creatures of Our God and King."

fork.setup: you're writing the guest list for a choir of praise. who makes the psalm's list?
options: angels, sea monsters, hail, cedars, kings and children.
fork.reveal: everything. heaven first, then earth, then every kind of person, old and young, side by side.

original.note: Hebrew: great sea creatures, the King James Bible's dragons. the same word as Genesis 1:21.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful psalm for nature lovers.
what it means: a roll call from the sky down to the ground, calling everything that exists to praise by being itself.
what a scholar hears: tanninim, the sea monsters of Genesis 1:21, are in the choir; the Benedicite in Greek Daniel and Francis's Canticle echo the same list.

notes: Tanninim in Psalm 148:7 and Genesis 1:21 (KJV 'great whales'). Confirm.

The Song of the Three Young Men (Daniel 3:52–90 in Catholic numbering) is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; the Benedicite is a canticle in the Book of Common Prayer. Confirm wording 'calling on everything from frost to whales'.
Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures, c. 1224–25; 'All Creatures of Our God and King' is William Draper's English paraphrase (early 20th century). Confirm.
The screen line 'PRAISE YE THE LORD' is KJV's rendering of Hallelujah at 148:1 and 148:14.
